questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: Explain what cross-cutting makes available to an audience
questions.stem: I noted in the log that the film showed two hives at once, the beekeeper at one and the robbers at another; explain what that technique makes possible.

answer.exemplar: Cross-cutting lets the film hold two actions in view as simultaneous, so the audience reads them against each other rather than in sequence. Because the cutting alternates between them, the film creates the impression that events in one place are causing or delaying events in the other, even when no one in either scene knows about the other. The device therefore makes simultaneity legible without exposition and lets the audience assemble a cause that the characters never state aloud.

questions.explanation: Cross-cutting holds two actions in view as simultaneous and invites the audience to connect them. The impression of cause comes from the cutting, not from anything the characters say.
questions.hint: Consider what the audience assembles from the two strands.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: Comic and grave register in one scene
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a scene holds a comic and a grave register together
questions.stem: I wrote in my log about the scene where a beekeeper jokes about a swarm while the old queen dies; explain how one scene holds both registers.

answer.exemplar: A scene can hold a comic and a grave register at once when the joke and the grief belong to the same set of people and the same moment, so that the laughter and the loss press on each other rather than alternate. The beekeeper's joke about the swarm is a defence against the fact of the dying queen, and the audience hears both the wit and the wound in the same breath. Nothing signals where the comedy ends, so the tonal shift is a matter of pressure between the two, and the scene stays funny and terrible at once.

questions.explanation: When the comic and the grave belong to the same situation, the two registers press on each other and both stay legible. Nothing signals a boundary, so the tension comes from the overlap rather than a switch.
questions.hint: Consider what the joke is doing about the grief.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a montage sequence makes elapsed time perceptible
questions.stem: I noted that the film spent eight seconds on a hive growing heavier from June to September; explain what the device does with time.

answer.exemplar: Montage makes elapsed time material rather than something the audience must count. By cutting between images whose differences carry the passage of weeks, the film compresses a long stretch into a handful of seconds and lets the viewer read duration from change rather than from narration. The weight of the hive becomes the measure of the season, so the passage of time arrives as a visible fact about the work rather than as information delivered about it, and the sequence also sets a rate of attention, since the audience is asked to compare images quickly.

questions.explanation: Montage makes elapsed time visible through change, so the audience reads months from a few images. It does not narrate the passage or require the viewer to count days, so the compression is perceptual rather than stated.
questions.hint: Consider how the audience knows time has passed.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: Explain how framing changes what an audience can judge
questions.stem: I shot the guild meeting twice, once wide and once in close shots on the speaker; explain what the close version changes for the audience.

answer.exemplar: The close version changes the audience's position in the room rather than the room itself. Held near the speaker, the audience loses the sense of who else is listening and how they react, so the words carry the whole weight of the speech and the speaker's composure becomes the thing under examination. Shot wide, the same speech would be read as one event among several, with glances and shuffles supplying the context. Framing therefore decides whether a moment is a public act or a private trial, without altering a word of it.

questions.explanation: A close shot removes the room and its reactions, so the audience examines the speaker instead of the occasion. Framing decides whether a moment reads as public or private without changing the words.
questions.hint: Consider what the wider shot would have shown instead.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: Prose scene and the play's rhythm
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a change of form changes the speed of a scene
questions.stem: I asked why the dramatist wrote the market scene in plain prose while the guild scene is in verse; explain the rhythmic effect.

answer.exemplar: The change of form lets the play vary its pace at the level of a scene rather than a line. Set in verse, the guild scene carries its business at a formal, measured gait appropriate to a body debating its own standing; set in prose, the market scene lets the talk break into shorter, quicker exchanges and lets interruption and noise pass through the lines. The audience hears the difference as a change in speed and formality before any subject matter is registered, which is why the two scenes feel like different kinds of time as well as different kinds of place.

questions.explanation: Prose and verse give a scene different speeds, so the formal business and the quick talk sound different in kind before their subjects are registered. The effect is rhythmic, not a change of plot or status.
questions.hint: Consider how fast each scene asks to be read.

questions.learningObjective: Explain what straight delivery does to the audience's judgement
questions.stem: I noted that the aside in our production was delivered flat and unsmiling; explain what that manner of playing achieves.

answer.exemplar: Playing an aside straight refuses the wink the audience expects, so the remark is received as a person's unguarded thought rather than as a signal that the author wants them to enjoy the moment. Without the comic inflection, the audience must decide for itself how much weight the aside carries, and that decision becomes part of the scene's meaning. The device keeps the judgement with the audience: the aside can be bitter, fond, or anxious, and the tone the actor withholds is exactly what the spectators supply for themselves.

answer.exemplar: Short clipped prose gives a scene the rhythm of quick transaction, and the choice is doing characterisation as much as pacing. Where the guild scene's measured lines let a speaker circle a point, the clipped sentences of the market let people finish, agree, and leave, which makes the trade in the scene feel brisk and slightly hollow. questions.stem: I wrote in my log about the scene where a novice tells a joke at the apiary gate while the queen is caged; explain the tonal design.

answer.exemplar: The scene works by refusing to separate its comic business from its grave fact. The novice's joke about the caged queen is told to a gate full of people who know exactly what the caging means, and the laughter that follows is not naive but nervous, which is what allows the scene to stay honest. Because the same fact that makes the moment funny also makes it brutal, the audience is never allowed to relax into the joke alone, and the tonal design holds two readings at once without ever announcing that it is doing so.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: Prose scene and the play's rhythm
questions.learningObjective: Explain what a change of form does at the centre of a scene
questions.stem: I asked why the play moves into prose precisely when the keeper reads the letter; explain the effect of that choice.

answer.exemplar: Dropping into prose at the reading of a letter changes what the audience does with the information. In verse the letter's words arrive already shaped by the play's formal purpose, while in prose they arrive as plain report, and the plainness makes them feel like evidence rather than as commentary. It also slows the moment, since a line of prose takes longer to read and absorb than a metrical line, so the audience keeps pace with the keeper's difficulty in holding the page steady. The change of form therefore marks the letter as the centre of the scene.

questions.explanation: Prose makes the letter's words read as plain report rather than as shaped commentary, and it slows the audience's pace to match the keeper's difficulty. The change of form marks the letter as the scene's centre.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: Prose scene and the play's rhythm
questions.learningObjective: Explain the effect of matching a scene's form to its length
questions.stem: I asked why the play's short scenes are written in prose while the long scenes are in verse; explain the effect.

answer.exemplar: Tying the form to the length of the scene lets the playwright control pace through the shape of the sentences themselves. The long scenes, with their measured lines and their weight of argument, give the audience time to hold a position being argued out, while the short prose scenes arrive and depart quickly, so the transitions in a life feel as brief as the form suggests. The audience registers the difference before it understands any content, and the change in form becomes a way of marking the difference in how much time a moment deserves.

questions.explanation: Matching form to scene length lets the shape of the sentences control the pace the audience experiences. The change is registered as rhythm before it is understood as content, so it marks the weight of a moment.
questions.hint: Consider what the line length does to the pace.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: Determine what a repeated image leaves the audience to supply

stimulus.body: The sequence shows the keeper tying a label to a jar, then cutting to a jar on a shelf in a different room, then to the same jar on a table with a new label. The shots are short and the jar's position in each frame is identical.

questions.stem: I noted this in my logbook; what does the sequence give the audience?

options.text: A single uninterrupted action seen from three angles at once
options.misconception: reads three separate views as one continuous shot

options.text: A precise count of the days between the labelling and the shelving
options.misconception: measures exact time the images cannot support

options.text: Proof that the jar was moved twice by two different people
options.misconception: turns a visual pattern into an account of agents

options.text: Three separate moments whose relation the audience must supply from the matching image

questions.explanation: Keeping the jar identical in each frame gives the audience a stable reference while the time between the views stays unstated, so they must construct the relation. The shots are separate, no days are counted, and no agents are named, so A, B and C overread them.
questions.hint: Consider what stays the same across the three views.
